summary: A 1979 list of assigned numbers used in network protocols. It replaced RFC 755 and was replaced by RFC 762. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: A big list saying which number means which thing in the network's rules. It was later replaced by a newer list.

questions: what port number is telnet in rfc 758
subtitle: Registry of numbers assigned for use in internet protocols and networks

tldr.problem: Network protocols need standardized numeric identifiers for various resources: network names, IP versions, protocol numbers, ports, and link numbers. Without central assignments, conflicts and confusion would result.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 758 lists all officially assigned numbers as of August 1979, covering network numbers (0-255), IP versions (0-15), protocol numbers (0-255), port/socket numbers (0-255), and link numbers (0-255).
tldr.outcome: This was the canonical registry for early Internet infrastructure. As protocols evolved, the registry was periodically updated; RFC 762 provided the next revision.

today: RFC 758 is Historic. It was replaced by RFC 762, which continued the evolution of assigned numbers. The practice of maintaining centralized registries for protocol numbers continues today through IANA.

sections.title: The Need for Assigned Numbers
sections.content:
Network protocols use numbers to identify many different things: which network a packet belongs to, what version of the Internet Protocol is being used, what protocol comes next (TCP, UDP, etc.), which port a service listens on, and what type of link a message is using. This RFC documents all the official assignments as of August 1979.

Jon Postel at USC-ISI maintained the registry and issued new assignments upon request. The document notes that the assignments should continue to be updated periodically.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocols use numbers like house addresses so packets know where to go and which service to ask for. Someone has to keep the master list so no two houses get the same number.

sections.title: The Main Categories of Assignments
sections.content: The RFC covers several categories of numbers. Network numbers (8 bits) identify different networks (ARPANET is 10, SATNET is 4, etc.). IP protocol versions (4 bits) define versions of the Internet Protocol; version 4 is the August 1979 standard. Protocol numbers (8 bits) identify what comes after the IP header (TCP is 6, UDP is 17). Port and socket numbers (8 bits) name the end points of logical connections (Telnet is 23, FTP is 21). Link numbers (8 bits) in the host-IMP interface distinguish different types of messages, with link 0 reserved for control and links 2-71 for ordinary data.
sections.plainLanguage: Different parts of the network have different numbering systems: which network, which protocol version, which protocol, which service port, and which type of connection. The document lists what each number means.

sections.title: Status and Evolution
sections.content: RFC 758 supersedes earlier registries including RFC 755, 750, 739, 604, 503, 433, and 349. It was published in August 1979 as both an RFC and as IEN 117 (an Internetwork Experiment Note). The document is careful to reserve ranges for future use and to mark some numbers as experimental. Since protocols and networks continued to evolve, this registry was intended to be updated periodically, and RFC 762 provided the next published revision.
sections.plainLanguage: This was a snapshot of all the number assignments in late 1979. As the network grew, the list had to be updated with new protocols and services, so later documents continued the work.

items.title: IP Versions
items.text: 4-bit field; version 4 is the August 1979 standard.

items.title: Protocol Numbers
items.text: 8-bit field in IP header (e.g., TCP = 6, UDP = 17).
